Consult Summary:
- Adult with known atopic eczema reporting an acute, widespread itchy, sore, dry rash (worst in antecubital fossae) worsening over the past few days; clinician prescribed oral antihistamine (fexofenadine) and topical mid‑potency steroid (Betnovate) with continued emollients.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Widespread sore, red, very itchy, dry skin involving chest, hands, arms; worst on the inside of the elbows (antecubital fossae).
- Timeline / course:
  - Symptoms present on a background of chronic eczema; described as "way worse" over the past few days (acute exacerbation).
- Exacerbating / relieving factors:
  - Patient continues baseline emollients (Diprobase) and uses Dermol in shower; has been using OTC hydrocortisone (low potency) without improvement.
  - Tried an OTC antihistamine (patient likely cetirizine) previously; patient reports it did not help.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - Reports skin cracking/fissures in affected areas.
  - Denies weeping/oozing from lesions.
  - Denies fever, joint pains, or other systemic symptoms.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No visible scratch marks reported.
  - Patient does not recall skin thickening/lichenification.
  - No change in current skin products reported (per patient).

Past Medical History:
- Atopic eczema (chronic), recurrent flares.
- Asthma — intermittent, uses blue inhaler PRN for flares.
- Family history: mother with hypothyroidism and migraine.

Medications:
- Diprobase (emollient) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Dermol (used in shower) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- OTC topical hydrocortisone (low potency) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- OTC antihistamine previously tried (likely cetirizine) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- PRN salbutamol (blue inhaler) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- New prescriptions discussed: fexofenadine (oral antihistamine) — dose/route/frequency not documented; Betnovate (betamethasone valerate) topical — apply twice daily as discussed (topical; strength/name documented; specific dose/FTU guidance: "small amount — one fingertip unit to cover palm/back of hand" provided).
- Allergies: None reported.

Social History:
- Lives in London; address provided (Sixty Hanover Steps).
- Occupation, smoking, alcohol, and substance use not documented.

Family History:
- Mother: hypothyroidism and migraine.
- No other relevant family history documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded (no clinician-performed exam documented; patient-reported skin findings recorded in History).

Investigations:
- None ordered or reported.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Acute flare of atopic dermatitis (atopic eczema) on background of chronic eczema, most likely cause of current widespread itchy, dry, sore rash.

DDx Integration (brief):
- 1) Atopic eczema flare — High likelihood.
  - Supporting: known chronic eczema, typical flexural distribution (antecubital fossae), intense pruritus, recent acute worsening.
  - Opposing: no clinician-documented exam or objective photos; no lichenification described.
- 2) Inadequate topical steroid potency / treatment failure — Medium likelihood.
  - Supporting: patient using OTC hydrocortisone with no improvement; clinician plans to escalate to Betnovate.
  - Opposing: adherence/application technique not fully documented.
- 3) Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis — Medium likelihood.
  - Supporting: acute worsening, involvement of hands/forearms, ongoing topical product use.
  - Opposing: patient denies recent change in products; distribution and history favor atopic eczema.

Issue 1: Acute atopic eczema flare
- Assessment:
  - Acute exacerbation of chronic atopic dermatitis causing widespread pruritus, erythema, dryness and focal fissuring; no signs reported of active weeping or systemic infection.
- Plan:
  - Prescribe topical betamethasone valerate (Betnovate) cream — apply topical twice daily to affected areas for a short course (clinician instructed twice daily; fingertip unit guidance provided). (Topical route and frequency documented; specific dose/FTU given verbally.)
  - Prescribe oral antihistamine fexofenadine for symptomatic relief of itch — fexofenadine prescribed (dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript).
  - Continue emollients: Diprobase and Dermol (continue regular use).
  - Safety-netting: Return earlier if symptoms worsen, develop weeping/oozing, signs of infection, or if adverse reaction to medications occurs.
  - Follow-up: If no improvement after the prescribed course (approx. 2 weeks as discussed), contact service for reassessment.
  - Prescription sent to Boots pharmacy for collection (clinician action documented).

Issue 2: Inadequate prior topical therapy / management optimization
- Assessment:
  - Patient has been using low-potency OTC hydrocortisone without benefit; escalation warranted.
- Plan:
  - Escalation to mid‑potency topical steroid (Betnovate) as above; provide application instructions (small amount, fingertip guidance, twice daily).
  - If poor response to appropriate potency/regimen, consider further review for adherence, secondary infection, allergy testing, or specialist dermatology referral.

Issue 3: Rule out secondary infection / other contributors
- Assessment:
  - Secondary bacterial infection considered less likely at present (patient denies weeping, crusting, fever), but eczematous skin with cracks is at risk.
- Plan:
  - Monitor for new signs: increased pain, purulence, crusting, spreading erythema, fever — if present, seek urgent review.
  - If no improvement after 2 weeks or clinical concern for infection, arrange in-person assessment and consider swab or empirical oral antibiotics per local guidelines or dermatology input.

General plan items:
- Continue PRN salbutamol (blue inhaler) for asthma as needed; no change to asthma management documented.
- Prescription dispatched to Boots; patient advised to collect.
- Education: continue emollients, use topical steroid as instructed, avoid known irritants; seek earlier review if worsening or adverse effects.

Quality checks:
- Missing but expected elements: no clinician-recorded vital signs, no documented physical exam findings or photographs, no smoking/alcohol/occupation history, no exact medication doses recorded for most meds.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified — DDx aligns with transcript findings and clinician plan.
- Transcript quality: Some brief inaudible exchanges; patient location and DOB partially confirmed; names of specific previously used steroid and antihistamine not fully specified by patient (uncertain).
